question.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{x\sqrt{y+z}-1}{{x}^{2}(y+z)-1} & =\frac{1\sqrt{2+(-1)}-1}{({1}^{2})(2+(-1))-1} \\  & =\frac{1-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{x\sqrt{y+z}-1}{{x}^{2}(y+z)-1} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{(x\sqrt{y+z}-1)(x\sqrt{y+z}+1)}{({x}^{2}(y+z)-1)(x\sqrt{y+z}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}(y+z)-1}{({x}^{2}(y+z)-1)(x\sqrt{y+z}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}(y+z)-1}}{\cancel{({x}^{2}(y+z)-1)}(x\sqrt{y+z}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{y+z}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2,-1)}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{y+z}+1} & =\frac{1}{1\sqrt{2+(-1)}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}.$
